speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: BOMARC MISSILE
speechtext: I should like to direct a question to the Minister of National Defence arising out of a radio report from Washington this morning by James M. Minifie. Will the minister comment on the report that in the next 30 days the United States will examine and decide whether or not to proceed with the installation of Bomarc missiles, and inform the house whether or not Canada is re-examining its policy with reference to Bomarc installations?

speakeroldname: Hon. G. R. Pearkes (Minister of National Defence):
subtopic: BOMARC MISSILE
speechtext:
Yes, Mr. Speaker, I heard the report over the radio this morning, and I understand
there is a re-examination or reappraisal of the situation going on. The military situation is always being reviewed.

subtopic: BOMARC MISSILE
speechtext: Will Canada's policy in this regard automatically follow whatever decision is made in the United States as a result of this re-examination?

subtopic: BOMARC MISSILE
speechtext: No, it will not automatically follow. Canada arrives at her own decisions in these matters. Naturally, as we are in a defensive agreement with the United States known as NORAD, we shall discuss with the United States authorities the implications of any changes which may be made.

subtopic: BOMARC MISSILE
speechtext: It would not be possible or practical though, would it, for Canada to proceed-

subtopic: BOMARC MISSILE
speechtext: Order.

subtopic: BOMARC MISSILE
speechtext: -with Bomarc installations if the United States dropped its policy in this regard?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: BOMARC MISSILE
speechtext: I think the hon. member is really engaging in argument on the subject rather than asking for information.

subtopic: BOMARC MISSILE
speechtext: May I put my question in another way. Is it possible for Canada to have an independent policy so far as Bomarc missiles are concerned if the United States decides to drop the Bomarc?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: BOMARC MISSILE
speechtext: It seems to me the hon. member's question is very like the second one he asked.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I think it is an important question. If your interpretation of the minister's answer is correct, then I am prepared to drop my question. My question is this. Is it possible for Canada to have an independent policy if the United States should drop the Bomarc missile?

speechtext: The house resumed, from Monday, January 25, consideration of the motion of Mr. Emilien Morissette for an address to His Excellency the Governor General in reply to his speech at the opening of the session, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Pearson, and the amendment to the amendment of Mr. Argue.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last evening when I had the privilege of adjourning this debate I had the privilege to relate to the house the unrest and uncertainty that existed in the minds of my constituents who are composed of workers, farmers and small business people. Of this I gave some evidence, and said it was the responsibility of the present government, and further

that the principles applied in Canada today by the present Conservative government resemble very much the principles applied by the administration of Mr. Bennett some 25 years ago.
May I this morning, Mr. Speaker, add further evidence to support my contention. We have heard-and it was with some surprise that many members of this house heard it a couple of days ago-about some form of amalgamation of our railway systems in Canada. As a young boy I recall that in the days of Mr. Bennett that was a problem that was discussed very much in this country. However, today it might be slightly changed. This government might possibly be introducing what they may call a gradual amalgamation of the railways. We were informed a couple of days ago that the telegraph offices of our two railway systems were being amalgamated at this time. This, no doubt, is of great importance to many workers in this country, and I feel that this government has a responsibility to study this major problem if it does exist, and to properly inform this house.
I had something to say as to the situation of the farmers in Canada and the price-cost squeeze of which we have heard so much. Yesterday I was much surprised when a member of parliament showed me statistics which, unfortunately, I had not the occasion to see previously. They were taken from the reports of the Department of Agriculture two days ago. The situation with regard to eggs in this country is most surprising. We are informed by these statistics that in the Ottawa area the farmers, the producers of Canada, are getting 24 cents a dozen for eggs and that, furthermore, in Edmonton 9 cents a dozen is being offered to farmers in that region for small eggs. If these problems continue I feel that possibly we shall see our own domestic products, our farm products, displayed in our stores and appearing as loss leaders. Undoubtedly this is a problem that this government should attend to immediately.
Then, of course, if we speak about workers and labour-management relations, we had the example a very few months ago of the handling of the civil servants' problem. How was that treated? I have in my own area some 500 civil service employees. They approached the management, which is no one but the government of this country. What was the reply; what was the policy expressed to the civil servants who were in a sense bargaining with their employer, the government? In that case there was no content; there was not even the usual package. We were informed that the main reason given was that an increase in civil servants' salaries might
The Address-Mr. Godin upset the budget of this government. That in no way can be a reply to the demands and the problem of the civil servants.
I do not know the details; I have not seen the report. The report was not made public. I feel that the government knows what is in the report. It is on the basis of the value of the arguments in the report that the decision of the government of this country should have been made, and not on the budget. When we are discussing the problems and the demands of the civil service the employer is the entire country, and no faction in the country should have to meet the deficit in the budget of the present Minister of Finance.
That was the argument, if you study it; that this might upset the budget. In other words the government is asking one section of the citizens of Canada to pay for the deficit which it has to meet.
We appreciated the comment made a few days ago by the Prime Minister to the effect that the prime minister of Japan had indicated that his country was willing to study the possibility of providing financial support for the establishment of industries in our country. However, we in the opposition feel that the government should take the lead in such efforts and indicate some willingness to develop our own industries rather than leaving it to strangers. It would be fatal if it should appear that the expansion of industry in our country was not being directed by the Minister of Trade and Commerce but by the Secretary of State for External Affairs.
I should like to bring to the attention of the house one fact in this regard. On February 8 nickel publicity week will commence. As I come from the nickel industry area I should like to bring this matter to the attention of members of the house so that within their own ridings they may do whatever they can to promote the use of this mineral. We are happy that we have this wealth, but we feel that before the Japanese are allowed to assist us in developing our industries the government has the first duty to assist in the expansion of industries in our country.

We can only expand if we find more markets and greater use for our production, and we should see to that ourselves. Consumers will benefit because we know that nickel is used as an alloy in many products such as steelwares; and monel metal, in the production of which nickel is also used, has brought much more comfort and convenience in our homes. Whether or not it is a good thing to receive a substantial capital inflow which allows Canadians to import and to proceed with the development of the economy at a faster rate than would otherwise be possible is a question upon which there may be differences of opinion.
However, in a period of world-wide shortage of capital and savings we should not complain about our almost unique capacity to supplement the savings of Canadians through borrowings in the United States market. At a time of rapid technological change Canada cannot afford to stand aside and refrain from the modernization of its plant and the development of its resources in accordance with the changing and growing requirements of domestic and world demand. Our investment in recent years has been sound and productive. Canadian businessmen have judged well the likely requirements of the future and have moved in good time to place themselves in a position to meet the new demands on our production.
The experience of the last 60 years has shown that Canada has had a foreign account deficit in periods of rapid expansion and a surplus in periods of depression or recession. Over the last 60 years, excluding 15 years as war and immediate post-war periods when trade was upset and the economy out of balance, the record shows that on commodity account Canada had deficits in 28 years and surpluses in 17 years. Almost all the years in which commodity account deficits were incurred were prosperous years for Canada, while most of the years showing commodity account surpluses were years of declining economic activity or general economic adjustment.
In 1912, for example, our adverse balance of trade was the largest in the pre-world war I period and amounted to over $283 million or $35 per capita. In 1956 our adverse balance of trade, the largest in the post-world war II period, was over $842 million or $50 per capita, and the depreciation of the dollar in the 44 years intervening would close the gap between those two figures. In the eight years 1932 to 1939 we had a succession of trade surpluses. The surplus reached its height in 1936 when it amounted to over $315 million, and Canada became a net exporter of capital. Imports varied from a total of $400 million to $800 million. Capital investment in 1939 was three-quarters of a billion dollars. Compare that with a capital investment of $8| billion in 1959. In 1939 unemployment, as a percentage of the labour force, was three times as great as it is now.

As I said elsewhere, I leave it to the economists to determine whether having a deficit in a period of economic expansion is as serious as is sometimes made out. That is why I have drawn attention to the period of the great depression when we could boast-if we could boast about anything-of a surplus and of being a net exporter of capital. I grant that the field of economics is a difficult one. I simply draw the matter to the attention of hon. members.
Imports have been high because of the inflow of foreign investment. This foreign investment in turn has made it possible for Canada to develop resources which could not have been developed with Canadian savings and enterprise alone. New branch plants have been established which are now producing commodities formerly imported. It is true that Canadians are acquiring new tastes and are continuing to buy more abroad, but as the domestic market for such commodities grows new branch plants as well as Canadian companies are likely to spring up to meet that growing demand.
Foreign capital, particularly from the United States and the United Kingdom, has played the major role in the development of a number of Canada's principal resource industries. I have three or four examples here to indicate that development. In the pulp and paper industry, for example, more than half the $1.6 billion invested is from abroad. The industry employs some 66,000 persons in pulp and paper mills, compared with 6,000 in the year 1900 and 31,000 in the year 1939. Corresponding new jobs have been generated in the related logging industry. Newsprint and pulp exports together provided over $1 billion worth of foreign exchange, or nearly one fifth of our total exports in 1959.
Foreign investment is also important in the petroleum and natural gas industry, which has attracted almost $5 billion. At the present time some 16,000 persons are employed in the oil fields and over 14,000 at refineries. Additional jobs have been created in connection with pipe line construction and oil and gas distribution. Prior to 1947 Canada was almost entirely dependent on foreign petroleum. The Canadian oil and gas industry now produces the equivalent of 70 per cent of our greatly expanded requirements. Exports of oil and gas in 1959 were valued at $90 million.
Another example of the importance of foreign investment to Canadian development is to be found in the iron ore industry. In the mid-1950's foreign investors committed sizeable sums in this industry and production increased from 6 million long tons 79951-0-22j
The Address-Mr. Churchill in 1953 to 20 million tons in 1956. Iron ore exports were valued at $31 million in 1953 and $145 million in 1956, and are estimated at $155 million for 1959 and will continue to rise.
Our internationally-known aluminum industry was established by foreign capital and still relies on foreign funds to a great extent. Eighty five per cent of this industry's production is exported, bringing in foreign exchange in excess of $200 million in each of the last four years.
Rising imports have made it possible for the Canadian economy to grow more rapidly than would have been possible otherwise. In fact total economic activity over the last five or six years has grown more rapidly than commodity imports. Between 1953 and 1959 commodity imports rose from $4.4 billion to $5.6 billion or $5.7 billion, or by 29 per cent. During the same period the gross national product rose from $25 billion to $34.7 billion, or by 39 per cent. The ratio of commodity imports to gross national product declined from 17.6 per cent to 16.4 per cent over this period.
Hence, any implication that productive capacity in Canada has not kept pace with the growth of imports is not borne out by the facts. On the contrary, rising imports made it possible for the Canadian economy as a whole to grow at an even more rapid rate than imports.
If we keep our own economy healthy and flexible and avoid the excesses of inflation or deflation, and if we aim to be competitive, our balance of payments will not cause insuperable problems; and I do not doubt the capacity of the economy to service the foreign debt which our borrowers have so far seen fit to assume.
It is worth remembering in this connection that in the 1920's our foreign debt relative to our national product was a good deal higher than at present. In 1926, for example, Canada's net international indebtedness was equal to the annual gross national product. In 1958, by contrast, our net international indebtedness had declined to two fifths of our gross national product. Moreover, exports of goods and services considered in relation to net foreign indebtedness have increased from about one third in 1926 to nearly one half in 1958.
On the subject of wheat the Leader of the Opposition was not on very familiar ground. He had little to say, but what he did say was rather confused and misleading. He left the impression that Canada was losing her position as a wheat exporter. Well, here are the facts, Mr. Speaker. When I first spoke of Canada's wheat economy in 1957 I discussed

The Address-Mr. Churchill at some length the surplus of 730 million bushels of wheat which was a cause for some concern. I pointed out that a long range view of Canada's wheat economy was the proper attitude to take in order to avoid undue alarm, and that a survey over a 30-year period indicated that periodically surpluses were accumulated but tended to disappear as conditions changed.
In the two crop years 1957-58 and 1958-59 the surplus has been reduced by almost 200 million bushels. In the present crop year a further reduction of the surplus will take place, and by July 31, 1960 it is unlikely that there will be many bushels of undelivered old-stock wheat on prairie farms.
Maintaining our export trade at a figure above, or close to, 300 million bushels has required vigorous action and constant attention. The wheat board and their agents have kept up their contacts with overseas buyers and have been alert to seize sales opportunities. In addition, the government has supported a large program of assistance to countries in need of food. That government program has provided in two years $46 million for gifts of wheat and flour to Colombo plan countries, and long term loans to those countries of $35 million. This substantial aid of over $81 million is not the whole story, but I might add at this point that it represents approximately 48 million bushels of wheat that have been moved from the prairies to these countries in need of food over the last two years.
In the same period the Export Credits Insurance Corporation, acting with government approval, has authorized insurance coverage of $22 million to assist in the financing of wheat and barley sales with three-year credit terms, and for the crop year 1959-60 these programs of assistance are being continued. Over $13 million has already been made available for gift purposes-I might say that not all of this has yet been taken up, but it is available-and a further $17 million has been authorized for insurance coverage to finance wheat and barley sales under the Export Credits Insurance Act. The major portion- that is 90 per cent-of our export trade in wheat continues to be sales for cash.
Canada has held her position-and I want to impress this upon the Leader of the Opposition-as the world's leading exporter of wheat in commercial markets. Canada's cash sales of wheat in the last crop year exceeded those of the United States by 125 million bushels. It is a confusing and misleading picture when you take just the total exports of wheat from other countries and place them against exports from Canada, and then infer that Canada has dropped in her position. It is


the great giveaway program of the United States which has so enlarged her exports. If we were able to match that with our treasury naturally we would continue to occupy, not only as a commercial salesman but as a donor country, the leading position in wheat exports. And let us not overlook the fact that thanks to the quality of Canadian wheat and the energy and initiative of Canadian salesmen and the Canadian wheat board, we are holding the leading position as exporter of wheat in commercial markets.
This is a creditable performance in a highly competitive field. World wheat production has increased considerably. The four major wheat exporters, Canada, United States, Australia and Argentina, do not have everything to themselves. France, Sweden, Italy, Mexico and Spain are also listed as wheat exporters under the international wheat agreement. In addition the U.S.S.R. has become active in the world's wheat market. Nor has there been any change in the situation I mentioned in 1957, namely that many importing countries continue to provide incentives for greater local production and maintain restrictions that limit the import of wheat. Developing markets in the countries of Asia and Africa provide hope for the maintenance of our export position as the populations of those areas enlarge their consumption of wheat flour.
In the chief and long-established markets of Europe we maintained our position in the crop year 1958-1959. Our exports of wheat and flour to the United Kingdom exceeded 100 million bushels. To West Germany we sold 35 million bushels as compared with 30 million in the previous year. Japan moved into second place with a purchase of 42 million bushels as compared with 39 million the year before. Those three major markets took 60 per cent of our wheat and flour exports. In other countries some gains were made and some losses were sustained. The longshoremen's strike on the west coast in August, 1958; the shortage of No. 5 wheat, the delay by Russia in taking up the balance of the shipments that we expected to make in the crop year-these three factors over which we had no control caused us to fall 6 million bushels below the target figure of 300 million.
In the new crop year 1959-60, of which nearly one half has already passed, our exports are running about 10 million bushels ahead of last year. What the final total will be no one can be sure. I express the hope that once again it will be at or near 300 million bushels. Every effort will be made to reach that figure but with increased world production, continued restrictive measures in some countries and the pressure in others to

dispose of surpluses, the obstacles are obvious and difficult. The high quality of Canadian wheat is the chief sustaining feature of our world wheat trade.
Mr. Speaker, I now turn to the question of the effects on our trade of the new trading arrangements in Europe. In the first place I wish to take the strongest exception to the Leader of the Opposition's view that for the past two years Canada has been entirely passive toward the new international trade developments in Europe. This is untrue. In the consideration of the European common market in GATT and elsewhere, Canada has taken a leading role in seeking to protect her trade interests in Europe, and in this we have co-operated with other outside countries whose trade might be affected.
A number of strong representations have been made directly to the common market countries in respect of access for Canadian goods. We have expressed particular concern about the agricultural policies to be adopted by the Six and the proposed level of the common tariff, including, of course, the tariff rates to be decided on for basic materials. We have been pressing the Six to adopt outward-looking commercial policies. There is now clear and welcome evidence in the statements of the European economic commission and of the governments concerned that it is their intention to move in this direction.
We have also been active in bringing to the attention of the United Kingdom authorities our interest in respect of the New European free trade association of the Seven. We have pressed for the elimination of barriers against our trade and for the maintenance of Canada's access to world markets. Given appropriate trade policies the potentialities for growth in Europe hold out the promise of substantially expanded Canadian sales to that area.
I might point out to the house that during the course of the last two years I have had the good fortune to meet the ministers of commerce in most of the countries of the Six and the Seven, those 13 countries in Europe that are so prominent in world trade. At every meeting we discussed the problem of trade between their country and Canada, and I received assurances from each minister I met that he and his country were in favour of expanding trade rather than restricting trade. That is why during the last while I have not expressed any despondency over the development of trading blocs in Europe, because I have had personal contact with the ministers of commerce in those countries.
Now, when you come to the bargaining table and documents are written and tariffs are being adjusted, there may be some areas
The Address-Mr. Churchill in which Canadian trade might be temporarily affected; but I repeat, as I have said before, that on a long range view Canada's trade will be enlarged because Europe is one of the great trading areas of the world and it cannot live by itself alone-because it does not have all the resources within its own boundaries-any more than the United States. And I would expect, the United Kingdom and western Europe being a great world trading area, that there would be just as much desire on their part to get into our markets as we into theirs. As their standard of living rises with increased trade, up will go their demand for goods and services from abroad. This is precisely what happened in Canada; as our standard of living rose, so our demand for goods and services increased.
Consequently, though we may view with alarm the formation of trade blocs, let us remember that we have presented the Canadian case directly to the people concerned. We have presented the Canadian case in the international form of GATT. The Minister of Finance and myself recently attended a conference in Paris where the Canadian case was again presented, and we will continue to present that case and to protect Canada's interests. Moreover, all those countries with which we are dealing are themselves signatories to GATT, which is an agreement calculated to reduce trade barriers throughout the world rather than to raise them. I do not want to take too optimistic a view of the situation, but I am certainly not pessimistic about it. Without doubt, western Europe and the Atlantic countries under the present arrangement will be in a much stronger position to face the competition which may come from other countries elsewhere; the iron curtain countries.
The house has already been informed of the recent conference at Paris at which machinery was established to deal with the substantial issues of trade which must now be faced as a result of European trade developments. In the further discussions which are about to take place concerning trade, aid and the refashioning of the organization for Europe an economic recovery we are entering upon a new course that may lead to a closer association with western Europe. We are prepared to play a more active part in new trading arrangements, provided no disadvantages result from such action; for although 30 per cent of our export trade goes to the United Kingdom and western Europe we have other important trade interests with commonwealth countries in the southern hemisphere and with Latin America and Japan. Mr. Speaker, I should like to associate myself with all hon. members who have extended congratulations to the mover (Mr. Morissette) and seconder (Mrs. Casselman) of the motion for an address in reply to the speech from the throne, and I should also like to offer my personal congratulations to our colleague from Quebec South (Mr. Flynn) on the confidence displayed in him by his leader and by the house in electing him as Deputy Speaker.
May I now point out that in the historic growth and development of our country an event of some significance was marked during the year 1959, when the Jewish community across the length and breadth of the country in every city, town and village where members of the Jewish community reside celebrated the bicentenary of their settlement in Canada. Distinguished recognition of the event was shown in the fact that the Prime Minister and all ten premiers of the provinces of Canada recognized this occasion and gave the celebrations their personal approval. I therefore desire to draw this event to the attention of hon. members and, indeed, to the attention of the entire country.
History records, in fact, that the first person of the Jewish faith to settle in Canada was a British officer named Aaron Hart, who came to Canada in 1759 with General Wolfe's army. He subsequently settled in what is now known as Three Rivers. It was his son, Ezekiel Hart, who in 1807 was elected from Three Rivers as a member of the legislative assembly of Lower Canada, but he could not take his seat because as a Jew he was obliged to take an oath on the true faith of a Christian which the statute at that time provided. He therefore did not take his seat.
A quarter of a century later, Mr. Speaker, and in fact 20 years before such an act was adopted by Great Britain, Canada passed the act of political emancipation which gave to people of the Jewish faith the same rights and privileges as those enjoyed by all subjects of Her Majesty the Queen. Since that

time the community has grown and prospered in Canada and now numbers a quarter of a million souls.
Celebrations were officially commenced on the afternoon of October 13, when the Governor General very graciously received a delegation of the Canadian Jewish Congress, who presented him with a beautifully illuminated scroll of a proclamation of faith and thanksgiving, which was issued in four languages, English, French, Hebrew and Yiddish. I now ask the indulgence of the house, Mr. Speaker, to read into the record this document entitled "A Proclamation of Faith and Thanksgiving on the Occasion of the National Bicentenary of Canadian Jewry":
The year 1959 marks the 200th anniversary of Jewish settlement in Canada where the blessings of a free country have made possible a flourishing Jewish community living in harmony with its fellow citizens.
From many lands, our people have come to these hospitable shores in search of religious and political freedom and economic opportunity. Thanks to these advantages, we have taken our place with our fellow citizens in the promotion of the economic, political, religious, social and cultural life of our country. We have come to the aid of the needy among us, and have brought relief to our brethren in countries of oppression and poverty. Our sons have responded to the call of patriotism in peace and war, some receiving coveted awards for their bravery and service, others making the supreme sacrifice.
In this mosaic of Canada we have held fast to our ancient prophetic ideals. We have been motivated by our steadfast belief in human dignity and human welfare. In this hour of thanksgiving we recall that our generation was privileged to witness the creation of the state of Israel, and we express our profound gratitude for the leadership Canada demonstrated in the historic achievement.
Therefore, with humility, the Canadian Jewish Congress does hereby proclaim this year as one of thanksgiving, prayer and celebrations to commemorate the national bicentenary of Canadian Jewry.
Let us give thanks to the Almighty for granting us the freedom to practice our beliefs, to transmit to our children our cultural heritage and to live in full equality with our fellow Canadians.
Let us pray, on this blessed occasion, for lasting peace in our country, indeed throughout the world, and for the happiness and prosperity for all that dwell therein.
It is signed by Samuel Bronfman, president, Canadian Jewish Congress; Lavy M. Becker, chairman, national bicentenary committee. This proclamation, Mr. Speaker, is a complete expression of gratitude, confidence and hope in the future growth and development of our country based on loyalty, democracy and freedom. I feel proud at this moment that I have had the privilege to place this expression and this document on the official records of our country.
Now, Mr. Speaker, it is a sad paradox indeed to have to draw to the attention of the house activities in Canada which threaten to mar that spirit of tolerance and understanding which our country enjoys. It is
The Address-Mr. Crestohl unfortunate that anti-Semitic manifestations in Germany and other countries have been permitted to spread to Canada. I hold in my hand, Mr. Speaker, a violently worded anti-Semitic message decorated with swastikas, iron crosses and other fascist symbols. Hon. members may look at it after the adjournment of the house if they wish. I particularly draw attention to the way this document is headed. It is entitled:
Eternal glory to the Fuhrer. Heil Hitler. Death to the inferiors.
It is signed:
A right wing group.
This was delivered to the residence of perhaps one of the most oustanding physicians in Montreal. I draw to the attention of the house, Mr. Speaker, the battle cry of this document, "Death to the inferiors." Again we have a proclamation, so to speak, of the superior race, the herrenvolk, as it was called. This seems to still be the dominating feature of this move, and is something that is rather dangerous.
I would like to point out to hon. members that the swastika is not only an anti-Semitic symbol, it is also in fact an anti-Christian symbol, as leaders of the Christian clergy have announced. It is so much an antireligious symbol that to my way of thinking it is an extremely anti-democratic symbol and is in fact a symbol which denotes antidecency, which certainly makes it anti-Canadian. For example, no Christian would smear the swastika, remembering the horrors that the swastika caused to Jew, Protestant and Catholic alike. Today it may be smeared on a synagogue, and if that is permitted, tomorrow it may be smeared on a church. It is a symbol of tyranny and terror, and should make us parliamentarians really deeply concerned that such a thing could possibly be permitted in this country above all countries.
Do not think, Mr. Speaker, that because I of the Jewish faith fear the resurgence of the swastika in Canada today, members of the Christian faith have no reason to fear its resurgence tomorrow. Just for an instant let us recall what the swastika has meant in Denmark, what it has meant in France, in Coventry, Lidice, what it has meant to Cardinal Faulhaber and Reverend Mr. Nei-moller, and the Catholics and Protestants who have suffered.
But, Mr. Speaker, while it was comforting to read the statements of the Prime Minister and the Leader of the Opposition condemning in forthright language the attempt to stir up in Canada a resurgence of this insidious Nazi propaganda; while it was also comforting to know that the press and the clergy throughout Canada vigorously condemned these activities,

The Address-Mr. Crestohl nevertheless I feel that the government should take some positive and direct action in a matter so dangerous to our country. If we are effectively to prevent this or any other type of sneak propaganda from spreading tyranny and hate I recommend to the government that they think seriously about enacting legislation which would impose severe penalties on those found guilty of actions of this kind. I do not think there is anything in the Criminal Code at the present time which could sufficiently, or even in any way for that matter, make punishable offences of this kind. I would suggest that the Criminal Code be amended to make a term of imprisonment mandatory. I think that would serve as some deterrent, though I do not think that in itself is a cure-all for this ill.
I consider the spreading of hate and violence as insidious as plotting the overthrow of government by force. Ultimately if such propaganda is permitted to penetrate into the vitals of the country, that too will be possible; therefore I consider them both treasonous acts. The fear of long term imprisonment would make these sneak culprits think twice and more before they would commit these crimes.
I do not want to suggest other remedies. I do not think any remedies can be suggested which could be a panacea to cure these things, but I do feel that members of parliament in their constituencies and in the house should in so far as possible encourage the educating of coming generations to understand that no one prospers by preaching hate, by preaching this form of animosity.
The program which the French television network had on Sunday night, I think, was the type of program which this country needs. I think it was educational. It was a splendid program directly on the point, indicating what sadness would result from these things and teaching the children of the coming generations the golden rule and to emphasize that the golden rule is not to be applied only to fellow Christians. I am certain that when the golden rule was preached it was intended to apply to all people of all faiths, because only then is it really a golden rule. I think such teaching is vitally important.
I also want to say that such organizations as the Canadian Council of Christians and Jews, where Christians and Jews meet together and get to know each other, are very helpful. Then also there is brotherhood week, which the Prime Minister endorses year in and year out, and the interfaith meetings that are held. I suggest these things to members of the house so that they may have them in mind. They are vitally important, and I think


we can perhaps look forward to a better future in our life in Canada if we live harmoniously together.
The hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Winch), I think, spoke yesterday about the various representatives of the commonwealth of nations who met in Australia. We met representatives there from South Africa, from India, from all parts of the commonwealth. We did not know them. The shades of skin were not like ours, but day after day we grew closer to each other. We ate with each other, we chatted with each other, we talked with each other, and after a short while no one even noticed that there was any difference of colour of skin or faith or religion or customs. We regarded each other as human beings, all children of the one God, and it was delightful to see the way we met and accepted each other's friendship.
I simply point out this fact to indicate that meeting and knowing people tells you at once that they are not always quite what you think. People are normal, people are fair, people are decent; but when opportunities are not provided to know each other all sorts of suspicions can creep in which should not. Therefore my appeal to hon. members is not because this propaganda is anti-Jewish or anti-Semitic-it is not only anti-Semitic, as I said a moment ago-but because it is a menace to the very security of our country, to the very security of our people, and all should combine and lend whatever support, assistance and thought they possibly can to see that evils like this are stamped out.
I should like to touch now on another matter. At the close of the last session I asked the Secretary of State for External Affairs whether Canada would raise its voice in protest to Egypt for not keeping the Suez canal open for all members of the United Nations. The minister then made the following rather patronizing statement, and I read from page 5746 of Hansard of 1959:
The hon. member is quite right. We place great importance on freedom of the seas. Of course this applies in the case of the Suez canal. Canada has always taken the position that there should be free transit of that canal. At the moment the secretary general of the United Nations is in the Middle East and is endeavouring to get this difficulty ironed out. We are hopeful that he will have some success in this endeavour.
Then I went on to say:
Has the government made its opinion known in this matter? Has it transmitted any protest to Egypt that it is in contravention of this undertaking to the United Nations?
The minister replied:
We have made it clear throughout all this difficulty that we place great importance on the right of free transit through the canal.
I point out that the minister still has not made a forthright declaration that Canada

has sent a protest to Egypt over the violation of the United Nations decision. I can understand the minister's reply. If I were to use legal language I would say that he avoided the issue. He dodged around the question. Perhaps there was some reason for him to do so at the time because, as he pointed out, the secretary general of the United Nations was then in the Middle East dealing with the matter.
But what has happened since? Has the secretary general of the United Nations achieved anything? I say that notwithstanding his efforts Egypt and certainly its leader, Colonel Nasser, have flaunted their failure to comply with the United Nations decision and, indeed, with international law that might apply in such cases. He continues acts of piracy by seizing ships which fly the flags of member nations.
I would have liked to hear the voice of Canada raised in very direct protest to inform Egypt that Canada objects to the manner in which it deals with international shipping and with an important international waterway of the world. This protest has not yet come from Canada. The Prime Minister of India, on the other hand, was not silent on the matter. As recently as two weeks ago he courageously reiterated India's belief that Israel's ships have a right of passage through the Suez canal, and went so far as to state:
If the existing situation militates against the interests of the parties concerned, we would follow the advice of the United Nations secretary general and evoke the operation of the international court.
I think, Mr. Speaker, it would do our country's prestige some good, if not much good, if, consistent with the minister's statement, a direct protest were to be sent to Egypt. Unfortunately time does not permit me to go into too much detail about the nature and extent of the piracy of which Egypt is guilty. It is a psychological truth, and I underscore this to hon. members, that the violation of the rights of one nation is bound to lead to violations of the rights of other nations, and since Canada uses the Suez canal we may be affected.
I feel it is our duty to speak up on this subject and not wait until we might be affected by some case of piracy, either by Egypt or by another country. It is always right to speak up courageously for justice rather than to sidestep it for a consideration, even if the consideration is the right of passage of oil tankers for any one country. Canada has always given leadership in championing the cause of right, truth and justice.
The Address-Mr. Crestohl
I had hoped that before approving the recent $56.5 million loan by the world bank to Egypt for the purpose of enlarging the very canal about which we are talking, we would have raised our voice in calling for respect for the decisions of the United Nations. Instead of that, what did we get? In reply to my question to the Minister of Finance as to whether or not there was a condition made before the loan was approved by Canada, we got the unwholesome attempt to involve a civil servant in voting approval of the loan. The government lacked the courage and the character our country has shown in the past when truth and justice clashed with expediency.
I wonder, even now, whether it is too late to realize that Colonel Nasser is playing both with Russia and the west and is actually getting the best of the two worlds. From Russia he asks for and gets money to build the Aswan dam; from the west he asks for and gets money to enlarge the Suez canal, yet daringly flouts the decisions of the United Nations. Canada has had an opportunity to raise its voice, but sadly has remained mute.
This is merely another painful illustration of appeasement. As recently as last week Sir Anthony Eden again very sharply deprecated the weakness and danger of exactly this type of appeasement. We apparently have not yet learned, and I am convinced that the free world threw away another opportunity to end the illegal blockade of the Suez canal when the world bank unconditionally approved the loan to Nasser.
What price appeasement, Mr. Speaker? The United States cries for freedom of passage, yet financially aids a country which violates the decisions of the United Nations to enlarge this canal. What a contradictory position for a country. What does Canada do? We simply follow blindly the contradictory position taken by the United States. I had hoped our government would have had more courage. Our country could have made a reputation in terms of truth and justice if it had at least spoken up. It could have said logically, "We sit on the world bank and we are asked to approve a loan, but we cannot and we will not give blanket approval to a country to do things, and continue to do them, in violation of United Nations decisions". I had hoped that Canada would have risen to that great height, and I am sadly disappointed that it did not.
As I should like now to touch on another subject, Mr. Speaker, may I call it one o'clock?
At one o'clock the house took recess.

At the adjournment I was on the point of speaking on the last item that I want to raise at this time, namely the problem of the immigration policy of the government. I do not think it is necessary for me to advance further my views on immigration. They are well known. I have done so during the past nine or ten years and I feel that there is no need, even at the present time, to urge the importance of an increase in immigration. I think that importance is fairly universally accepted. Certainly it is accepted by the government, judging by the language of the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration, the Prime Minister himself and other speakers on the government side. For example, the hon. member for Parkdale the other day delivered an excellent speech urging upon his government the importance of an increase in immigration.
I repeat that I think everyone in Canada agrees on this matter. Boards of trade, chambers of commerce and industry generally all favour increased immigration. What I am wondering is why no one does anything about the matter. We all shout that we want increased immigration, but everything seems to have bogged down. The figures show a decrease in immigration.
What lies behind this situation? I tried to fathom it but I could not do so. I do not know whether there is some group, some individual or some machinery which interferes with the process of immigration into Canada. Speaking for myself, I have reached the conclusion that the difficulty could be the Immigration Act itself. If the difficulty is the Immigration Act itself I think it is time the act should be revised.
On April 12 of last year, as reported at pages 2937 and 2938 of Hansard, the minister herself had this to say, and I now quote what she said with respect to the possible revision of the Immigration Act. These are the words of the minister herself:
I hope to suggest revisions to the act in a few months' time in any event.
In other words she was informing the house that she hoped to suggest a revision of the act-which is probably going on-very soon, but in a few months' time in any event. Then she continued as follows:
I trust the revisions which I will then propose will be understood and will have the approval of all those interested in immigration.
That was fine. That was in April of last year. More than a few months have elapsed since that time. With the minister knowing that the country is really pressing for a revision of the act, and also knowing that she

plans a revision of the act, why was there not a word of reference to that matter in the speech from the throne? Is it again a matter of not wanting to revise the act? Is it again the well known process of simply letting things ride?
Only the other day I again asked the minister whether or not there will be a revision of the act during this session of parliament, and she very glibly ducked from under by the well known method of informing the house that the matter is receiving the constant attention of the government and of the department. I do not think that is a satisfactory answer. If the only thing apparent at the present time that could be blocking immigration is the Immigration Act, I certainly think something should have been said about it in the speech from the throne, especially in the light of the minister's promise last year that the act would be revised in a few months.
I wonder also whether recent publicity in the press, which was not very complimentary to the department of immigration, should not be another spur to the Prime Minister and to his government to really look into the revision of the act. Certainly there has been some extremely painful publicity both for the department and for the government. In the light of these promises what I am wondering is this, and I return to this matter. Is there some influence that is holding up the revision of the act? May I just read one brief opening paragraph in an editorial of the Montreal Star of January 4, 1960 entitled "Time for Overhaul":
Without delay the Immigration Act should be reviewed and the operations of the department surveyed. Either, if not both, is in need of liberalization.
Of course I like the term "liberalization", but in any event the editorial continues as follows:
Arbitrary behaviour on the part of department personnel would lead one to think sometimes that they are constantly hostile to immigration. It is a question whether they should have the power of discretion they sometimes exercise.
I know the Prime Minister's generous view about this matter. With his sense of justice I feel that he could not fail to realize with regard to the Immigration Act, many sections of which he himself so vigorously criticized when he sat on this side of the house, that after three years in office with the power to alter those things which he criticized he has failed to take one single step to deal with those matters which he knows are faulty in the Immigration Act, and has so stated.
Everyone who has been reading the papers has read the observations of a judge of the supreme court of Ontario. I know this matter

is not new to the house, but in order to emphasize it I want to draw attention to it. In the case of Imre Hirsch, which was recently before the supreme court, here is what the judge said. I am now reading from a clipping from the Toronto Globe and Mail of December 31, 1959. Here is the quotation:
In an early brush with immigration department counsel John Hilton, who claimed his lordship was not empowered to hear the case, Mr. Justice Stewart replied: "If an asinine view is taken by an unqualified officer, you mean I can do nothing? If such a fundamental thing as natural justice is quite clearly denied I can surely do something about it."
That is a statement by an independent tribunal, the supreme court of Ontario. Surely when one reads an item like that it cannot possibly do the Prime Minister or the immigration department much good. I imagine he would feel a little embarrassed by a statement like that, and the Prime Minister should be the first one to look into this and say, "What is there in the act which could provoke a statement like that from a judge of the supreme court of Ontario?"
Then further on the following appears:
As a special inquiry officer, Mr. Gracie was pursuing his duty under the Immigration Act, he argued, and simply acting on his own opinion as he is entitled.
Mr. Justice Stewart promptly replied:
Can he be as arbitrary as he likes?-Yes, answered Mr. Hilton.
Then the judge, with almost absolute indignation, said:
You want the law interpreted in the lowest possible fashion on behalf of the special inquiry officers.
His lordship said such arbitrary discretion allowed officers was "perfectly shocking and disgraceful- against every conceivable thing since the Magna Carta and should be stamped out as vigorously as possible."
Mr. Speaker, I could pretty nearly let my case rest on this last statement in appealing to the Prime Minister, who should certainly recognize the poignant language of the judge. Since Magna Carta nothing like that has been heard of, and it arose owing to an interpretation of the Immigration Act. I do not want to use harsh language, but it is a disgraceful thing for the country when a judge so assesses the Immigration Act. However, there it is, and I think basically it is that which is at the bottom of holding up an increase in immigration to this country. Therefore I would ask the Prime Minister promptly to see to it, as did the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration herself, that all these faulty sections in the act which are repugnant to a sense of justice are immediately remedied by a revision of the act.

Mr. Speaker, may I join with previous
The Address-Mr. Grafftey speakers in this debate in congratulating the mover and the seconder of the address in reply to the speech from the throne (Mr. Morissette and Mrs. Casselman).

As to the Deputy Speaker, I wish to congratulate him on the great honour that was bestowed upon him.
This debate is of a particular importance. Indeed, what better way have we at our disposal to feel the nation's pulse than by listening to duly elected members from various districts from coast to coast?
Some of the problems brought up during this debate are of merely local interest, while others have national and even international significance.
Mr. Speaker, I had the opportunity, since this session began, to talk with some of my fellow citizens of Brome-Missisquoi, and several of them gave me then their impressions and opinions.
This is a good thing, Mr. Speaker. It proves that the Progressive Conservative government is close to the people of Canada. I said it before and I say it again: we are the party of the people and the voice of the people is our strength.
This is why our party attaches such importance to this debate on the speech from the throne.
Mr. Speaker, I realize that it is difficult to separate national issues from those of merely local interest.
As far as I am concerned I should like to deal not only with matters of particular interest to my fellow citizens of Brome-Missisquoi, but also with matters of concern to the people of Canada from coast to coast.
Let me therefore immediately take this opportunity to deal in particular with matters concerning Brome-Missisquoi, the riding of my fellow citizens, of my constituents.
(Text):
Mr. Speaker, so many of the accomplishments of our government are naturally brought about by legislation. So many of the accomplishments of our government are brought about by announcements on the part of the government in this very house. But some of the things I want primarily to talk about this afternoon come about gradually, perhaps imperceptibly, and are brought about by the attitude and mode of thinking of our government, of our party and the present administration.

The Address-Mr. Grafftey
One of the things I would primarily like to talk about is the attitude of our government to the commonwealth. I would like to point out the government's and our party's attitude to the commonwealth, this informal body of states. In my opinion, since our party has assumed office I have seen a new look, a new, positive, constructive look, of associated leadership on the part of Canada. We are all aware of the fact that the commonwealth of nations has always been and is being a great force for good in the world today. I would simply like to say that under the leadership of the Prime Minister, Canada has taken on a new, positive constructive role in the commonwealth of nations.
Would you permit me, Mr. Speaker, to put on the record some quotations from the book by D. Taylor called "The Years of Challenge". I would like to quote from his book the following passage:
The very day he was sworn in as prime minister he flew off to London to attend the meetings of the commonwealth prime ministers-Over and above that he had his own inspiring vision of a commonwealth growing ever more powerful in influencing the rest of the world. And he was prepared, even with his precarious majority, to add a decisive element of Canadian, leadership to that of Britain. He was prepared not merely to talk, but to act. It was this which made Diefenbaker a figure of incalculable significance, that he was eager to be actively responsible for the development of the commonwealth. This was precisely what had long been needed-a leader from the commonwealth who was prepared to make it the cornerstone in the development of his own policies, and not relegate it to a subsidiary position. In brief, it was not nearly enough to remove the word "British" from in front of "commonwealth" to demonstrate that all were equal. It was for the members of the commonwealth thenceforward to put as much into its development as Britain had done. Diefenbaker saw that. And he was prepared to do something about it-
The final quotation I would like to put on the record comes after the Right Hon. Prime Minister had spoken in Albert Hall in London during this first visit. He used the expression that the commonwealth has an appointment with destiny, and Taylor goes on to say:
A trite enough phrase, one of a hundred such which have too often in the past served to wrap the commonwealth in a platitudinous fog. But there was a difference this time. The difference lay not only in the sincerity but in the purpose of the man who uttered those words, and in the remarkable response of the people who listened to him. Led by the Prime Minister of the United Kingdom, Harold Macmillan, they stood to their feet, clapping for minutes on end. They sensed that the commonwealth was indeed reaching a stage in its development that would decide how great an instrument for the welfare of man it would be-
Mr. Diefenbaker set in train greater things than perhaps even he had dreamed of when he pressed for a commonwealth conference. For out of Montreal there evolved the idea of a joint attack on poverty by a free world. This had of course been dealt with in a million words before, even tackled on a moderate scale, piecemeal. But now there was

clear the pattern of a grand design, and that pattern became clearer soon after the world bank meetings in New Delhi. Briefly, it came down to this: the richer nations of the commonwealth (led by Canada and Britain), the United States and the wealthier countries of democratic Europe were pledged to raise the living standards of less fortunate lands. The grim and unremitting war between the two great political creeds of the world, democracy and communism, was to be fought out on the economic as well as the ideological front, and victory there was the first essential.
I put those quotations on record to show that even people abroad recognize the new role of associated leadership that Canada is playing in the commonwealth; a new, positive, and constructive role that I should like to underline in my remarks this afternoon. And we can be assured that under the leadership of the Prime Minister this role of constructive, positive leadership will be foremost in the minds of the present administration and the government.
Along with the very hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Chevrierl I had the pleasure of being invited this fall to a conference of parliamentarians at Clarens, Switzerland. I should like to stress that, like myself, all the parliamentarians present were merely speaking informally. We discussed many of the things that are concerning and influencing most of the nations of the world today. None of us, as I say, were speaking officially on behalf of our particular governments and I want to stress, before I make my brief remarks on this subject, that it was simply an informal meeting, informal conversations among members of parliament from various countries.

speechtext: Is that why you made such a good free trade speech?

speechtext:
I do not think I used the expression "free trade". The discussions were broken down under two general headings; first, the problem of armaments and, second, the problem of regional arrangements for European economic and political relationships. Under the first heading, armaments, we had the real pleasure of being addressed by Right Hon. Philip Noel-Baker, our principal speaker. Most hon. members of this house will know that he is this year's Nobel peace prize winner. Time and time again Noel-Baker stressed that in the twentieth century the imperative is disarmament. This has been, perhaps, the keynote of his life's work, and it was certainly the keynote of his speech to the conference.
At this point I should like to relate to the house some of the impressions I brought back home from those meetings in Clarens. Noel-Baker pointed out that he was really disappointed-and he was pointing his finger for the most part at the western nations-that

so many nations sent relatively minor officials to take part in disarmament talks and discussions. It is for this reason that I personally and, I am sure, many members of this house were very happy to find that General Burns has been named by Canada to take part in the disarmament negotiations which are to be held in Geneva. Certainly, in my opinion, work of this nature merits the attention, study and efforts of this eminently distinguished Canadian soldier and statesman. Noel-Baker went on to point out that although so much of the work which had been done at the old league of nations in connection with conventional disarmament ended up in failure, we would do well to consider the fact that many serious disarmament proposals were placed before the league, and it could yet serve a very useful purpose to look at some of the detailed proposals which were hammered out at Geneva in those days after a great deal of hard work.
I should like to say that in the field of nuclear disarmament there was a feeling at our meeting of cautious optimism that there might soon be an agreement covering inspection and the cessation of tests, but it was also pointed out that we should never lose sight of the real necessity for conventional disarmament as we became preoccupied-as well we might-with the problems of nuclear disarmament.
In bringing my remarks on this subject to a close I should like to say only that the fact that the western nations are conscientiously exploring all realistic avenues toward the realization of disarmament by no means implies that we are lessening our intention to be vigilant and strong at all times.
Under the heading "Regional Arrangements for European Economic and Political Relationships" we discussed, hon. members may rest assured, the problems of the European common market. We discussed the questions arising from the formation of the group of Six and the group of Seven, which have already been referred to at length by some of those who have taken part in the present debate. There was general agreement at our meetings that both these trading blocs or associations had very serious intentions; and it is my opinion, though I may be wrong here, that because of the balance of payments situation as related to these two groups it might be more than possible that in the future they will formulate some type of working agreement between themselves.
Naturally, from a Canadian point of view I took a great interest in these matters. I informed most of the people there that Canada as a signatory of GATT would be more than interested to see that the spirit of that agreement was always upheld. A question
The Address-Mr. Grafftey which I put to many of my friends at the meetings was this; how did they feel these new trading blocs could be prevented from becoming introspective and isolationist in nature, and the answer I generally received was that GATT was the best place in which to discuss these matters, and that GATT could be used as a forum for ironing out difficulties. It was stressed time and time again that we should not take a negative or defensive attitude toward these new economic blocs, but that if they were properly discussed in GATT or elsewhere trade co-operation in the world in general could be enhanced.
In spite of the fact that members of the opposition like to use the words "free trade" or "high protection" I myself prefer the middle of the road phrase "trade co-operation", believing it to be more realistic in this day and age. I often listen to the words of wisdom from the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickersgill) in particular when he likes to impose on this house the classical debate on high tariffs versus free trade. I say that such a debate might have been relevant in a bygone age but I feel that it has outlived its contemporary usefulness and, speaking personally, prefer the expression "trade co-operation". Multilateral and bilateral trading agreements realistically arrived at will lead us into an era of trade co-operation with nations which have had such a wonderfully happy and well earned economic advance since the second world war. As Canadians we cannot but be happy to see our allies advance economically in this way. Again I say that a spirit of trade cooperation will underline our efforts to work with these trading groups, which should be expansive and outward looking in nature.
Obviously in a debate of this nature I cannot go into the subject in any great detail, but at our meetings at Clarens we naturally discussed in some detail the effects and implications of Russian and communist trading on the world trade picture.
I should like to close my remarks on this particular subject simply by saying that as Canadians, amongst other things, we should consistently support our government's intentions, plans and present efforts to effect a policy of more goods produced by Canadians for Canadians. A government policy thus primarily directed at our secondary industries will help productivity, and aid our trading picture.
Sir, before going on to the next part of my speech, perhaps some hon. members may recall that unfortunately I had some altercation in the house with the hon. member for St. Jean-Iberville-Napierville (Mr. Dupuis).

The Address-Mr. Grafftey We are neighbouring members of parliament, sir, and we like to have the odd little debate in this house. I challenged him with a remark to the effect, what did he know about my constituency, then he put the question to me, "Well, how do the unemployment figures today compared with the day you were elected?" Well, sir, I can only say to the hon. member for St. Jean-Iberville-Napierville that it was a good question to ask. He gave me a little more work to do over the week end.

Many great Canadians in my province have had a lot to say about exactly what the Conservative party means when we talk about provincial rights. In England Disraeli, Burke and Coleridge, the moral philosopher of conservatism, spoke out against the Whigs and their centralizing tendencies in London.
Yes, sir, one of the main tenets of conservatism is a high regard for local selfagency. This regard, sir, is well received in my province. Burke's idea of "the happy platoon" stated that our immediate affections are borne in our families, in our neighbourhoods and in our provinces. This is the germ, as it were, of our broader affections. Sir, the citizens of my province love their province but that in no way lessens their real spirit of Canadianism. If in the past Liberal administrations stated that this meant a policy of unco-operative autonomy, so much the worse.
It has always seemed paradoxical to me that past Liberal administrations, the architects of dullness, attempted to superimpose a drab degree of uniformity on our Canadian way of life by their centralizing tendencies while on the other hand, at the local level, they preached a divide and rule policy of sectionalism. I have seen this game being played in this house and outside the house in relation to my own province and I saw it played in this house during the last session in relation to Newfoundland during the Newfoundland debate. Mr. Speaker, these differences constitute a real and fundamental difference between the two major parties in this house, and I feel it is a difference that all members should note.
Just the other night the Leader of the Opposition spoke to the Canadian nation about a distinctive Canadian flag; a laudable desire, a laudable subject, but do you think his desires are rendered any more easy to attain after speeches such as we heard from the
The Address-Mr. Grafftey hon. member for Hull (Mr. Caron) yesterday? I say no. This is the same old story. Time and time again we have had leaders of the Liberal party going out into the country and speaking about national unity, while the members of that party go back to their ridings and sometimes, as we saw the hon. member for Hull do yesterday, speak about that type of divide and rule sectionalism which does not enhance the possibility of uniting this country or obtaining the distinctive flag the Leader of the Opposition talked about.
The second subject I should like to talk about in my general remarks is the attitude of our party and government to the House of Commons in which we are debating this afternoon. We see that the rules of the house are coming up for review. We see the committee system working as it has never worked before. When our party assumed office we had a mandate to restore the legislative wing of government to its proper functions. While the separation of powers theory cannot be completely superimposed on the parliamentary system, we do know that our affairs are best governed when there is a healthy division between the legislative, administrative and judicial wings of government.
It has been said before in this house, and I will say it again, that our civil service is second to none in the world today. It is a good and great civil service, but no matter how good it is it should not and does not want to have what are essentially legislative functions. Before we came to office the voice of the people had been endangered by a government that had forgotten the people. Let us never forget that their very right to be heard in this chamber was being seriously challenged and endangered.
Today national interest in federal affairs is at an all-time high. This chamber is assuming its rightful functions. Members of parliament are working hard and doing their homework. But I well know, after listening to the debates last session, that often when members of parliament were advancing the true and legitimate desires and aims of their constituents, opposition members yelled, "Political interference, political interference". Very often when the government was performing its rightful legislative functions the opposition again yelled, "Political interference." I say, sir, that they are not serving well the true interests of this house if every time the government or private members try to perform their true and rightful legislative functions, opposition members shout indiscriminately "Political interference".
I will simply inform all members of the opposition that in this regard there will never be any gagging technique. The voice of the

The Address-Mr. Grafftey people will be heard by a House of Commons party, a House of Commons government, under the leadership of a House of Commons prime minister. I can certainly say that is one of the basic principles that will always be foremost in our minds as Progressive Conservative policy on the part of our party as our government leads the Canadian people into the decade of the 1960's.

I fully realize that those tests have caused temporary hardships for many farmers whose cattle have been condemned by the Department of Agriculture, but I am equally assured that all citizens of Brome-Missisquoi welcome the day when Bang's disease will be completely wiped out of our district and our two constituencies will be declared certified. In Farnham, the Department of National Defence maintains one of the finest military camps in the country. Especially noteworthy is the summer camp held for young cadets. So far as the seconder (Mrs. Casselman) is concerned, I should like to tell my hon. friend publicly, as I have already told her privately, that she certainly deserves all the sincere congratulations that were extended to her after her speech. I hope that we will have other opportunities of hearing her speak in French, because the French members of this house have noticed that her French is excellent and her pronunciation is very good. Again may I extend my congratulations. (Translation):
I also want, Mr. Speaker, to tender my congratulations to hon. members who, since the last session, were appointed either parliamentary assistants or ministers. I can assure them at this time of my best wishes for the work they are going to accomplish in their new functions.
With regard to the hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Flynn) who was just appointed Deputy Speaker, I want to tell him that I am happy about his appointment. I trust that, when discharging his responsibilities, he will mainly be guided by his sound judgment and fair mind.
It is now two and a half years Mr. Speaker, that the country's fate has been in the hands of this government. As a matter of fact, more than half the term of the legislature has passed since June 1957, which marked the advent to power of the Conservative party.
We may very well remember that after two electoral campaigns of belittling, filled with all sorts of promises, as glittering as they were hollow-supported by expensive organization and publicity-the people of Canada entrusted its lot to a Progressive Conservative government, and did so with an overwhelming majority. After the Canadian people had given them this token of confidence they were entitled to expect that the government's promises be kept. That was the hour of the great delusion.
For practically the past three years we have had a government which is very strong in the house but extremely weak and hesitant when any issue is to be settled. We were all anxious to find out from the speech from the throne whether the government was able to remedy these conditions, particularly with regard to tight money and high interests.
But no, the speech from the throne is very poor, and there is nothing in it that might

give the population which is so deeply affected, any confidence.
We are far from those days, where the Prime Minister roused his listeners, with his visions of the prosperity which would be theirs in Canada, when he would be in power.
After two and a half years of administration by this government, it will certainly be interesting to look at the record of the first part of their term of office, and, in order to do so, I believe it might be wise to recall some of the promises-not all the promises that were made, for their list would be too long-but some of the most important and significant ones which were given by that party in 1957 and 1958.
Here are some of them: "Tax cuts with a balanced budget." That has not been done.
"Increase in social security measures, without increase in taxation." That has not been done either.
"Interest rates cuts, especially for housing construction." On the contrary, they were increased. We then came to a period of tight money. Reference was made to "tight money policy", at the time of the Liberals, but credit today is more restricted than ever.
"Checking inflation." Yet the cost of living has constantly gone up since.
"Settling of fiscal problems with the provinces." Another point which is not settled; perhaps the provinces are waiting for an arbitrary decision by telegram.
"Financial help to municipalities." During the election, the Prime Minister told them he would grant them their share of taxation, especially to facilitate their rapid growth. Now our municipalities are not even able to borrow money.
"Settlement of the unemployment problem." Mr. Speaker we were promised that the unemployment problem would be solved; and you know the fine result we have had: there are now 700,000 unemployed.
"Opening of new markets for our products." That must have been also a vision, because we do not see many new ones.
"Better protection for our sovereignty, especially as opposed to the increasing United States influence in Canada." In his speech this morning, the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Churchill) showed, in this regard, what I would call the best example of turnabout one could imagine.

I shall therefore limit myself today to the discussion of two or three matters which, in my opinion, are of particular interest to the major part of the population.
May I first be allowed, Mr. Speaker, to discuss the promises made by the Conservatives to the effect that they would reduce taxes while balancing the budget.
Memories are still ringing with the charges hurled at the Liberal administration, in the year 1957 and also in 1958 and during the elections, to the effect that the Liberal government of the time was robbing every family of $120 a year-
