speechtext: The hon. member is asking for the reference from which the hon. member wishes to read.
I thought I gave it rather clearly. It is the Canadian Medical Association Journal, volume 81, December 1, 1959, page 958.
You had better tell him the line.
It is the seventh paragraph in the lefthand column.
It would be the left.

Reading from here and so
that my hon. friend, who I understand is a doctor-
You understand correctly.

Many of our understandings are correct as time has proven time and again. Because the hon. gentleman has raised this question I feel I am obliged to read the entire paragraph, Mr. Speaker, which I did not intend to do.
Could you read the entire article?
I will gladly read the entire article.
Do so.
However, I am sure that someone would then raise the question that I was reading my speech.
Well, that is true too.

I quote:
A development which will be of interest to doctors as well as to the public at large is the possibility that the pharmaceutical profession-
He has not given the author of the article.

I continue:
-will bring forward a "prescription insurance" scheme whereby any individual or family may, by payment of a monthly fee, receive all prescriptions free. The pharmacists estimate that 30 per cent of prescriptions given to patients are never filled, largely because of the increasing costs of drugs. There is at present one such scheme in operation in Canada, at Windsor, Ontario. The British Columbia pharmaceutical association discussed this at their annual council meeting October 25 to 27.
End of paragraph, end of the entire reference.
Could the hon. member give us the author?

I would be glad to oblige my friend by answering his questions when I conclude my remarks. I only have a few minutes left and I want to get in as much as possible of what I wish to say before my time runs out. I am sure my hon. friend will appreciate the need for doing that.

One of the major arguments used by the pharmaceutical industry to justify the charging of these high prices is that initially they have high research costs which must be recouped and the only way they can get back these expenditures on research is by charging higher prices to the consumers. I have another reference here which should indicate that maybe the research costs about which the pharmaceutical industry talks so much are not in fact valid figures at all. This is a quotation from an address by Mr. Chet Shaw to the American drug manufacturers' convention in 1956. With respect to the boasted $100 million research figure he said:
We've done lot of talking about an estimated $100 million, but we'd be hard put to document it. What if someone questioned it-someone whose voice we couldn't afford to ignore?
In the antibiotics field the price of antibiotics has not changed one bit since 1951. Even though there has been a tremendous increase in the volume of sales the prices set at the manufacturers' level and suggested list prices have remained identical over a period of nine years both here and in the United States. The price set in 1951 designed to recoup research costs has not declined but has remained static even in spite of the tremendous increase in the volume of sales, even in spite of the entry of newly developed antibiotics into the field at the same level established in 1951. This should indicate that there is a conspiracy to set prices in the field of antibiotics and the drug industry generally. It suggests that Cyanamid of Canada, Bristol Laboratories, Pfizer Corporation, E. R. Squibb and Upjohn are part of this conspiracy to establish unnecessarily exorbitant and high prices in the antibiotic field. In fact, there is a court case on this very subject matter right at the moment.
Unfortunately, I think because of their silence, the pharmacists in the nation, who should know and do know a great deal more about this subject than do most other people, are being branded as one of two things: one, as apologists for the price-fixing manufacturers or, two, they are being looked upon by the general public as the persons mainly responsible for the high cost of drugs. What happens psychologically when an individual takes a prescription into a drugstore? He pays whatever may be charged, $10 or $12, and he relates the money he pays to the pharmacist and says the pharmacist is the person responsible for the high cost.
We know full well that when we are ill we are concerned with getting well, and we are concerned with paying whatever costs are charged to us for whatever particular drugs are prescribed by the doctor. This drug piracy must be discontinued. There is no question but that drug prices, particularly
The Address-Mr. Allard the prices of the antibiotics to which we are referring here, could be cut in half without in any way affecting the income picture or position of the particular manufacturer within the industry. When United States parent companies of Canadian subsidiaries can in one year make up to 40 per cent profit on their sales there is something-well, one could find some harsh words to apply, but it does not sound sensible or reasonable that this sort of profit picture should be allowed to continue.
I know there is an investigation being conducted, so far as we can ascertain, under section 42 of the Combines Investigation Act, a so-called research project. So far as I am able to gather, a report may be made within three or four months. The study has been taking place within the combines branch for some two or three years. I hope that when the report is made it will be such a comprehensive report and in such detail as to show the true picture of the drug manufacturing industry in this nation.
Those are all the remarks I wish to make in this particular debate, Mr. Speaker. If my friend wishes to ask questions, as he indicated earlier he did, I shall be glad to make an attempt to answer them.

The hon. member who has
just concluded his speech has asked if there were any questions. I have a list which is rather lengthy, and I am afraid I would have to look at the written word before I could ask intelligent questions on the many extravagant, and I think erroneous, statements that have just been made.

There is one good thing, we can have differences of opinion.
(Translation):

Mr. Speaker, I admire your alertness in so quickly recognizing the members who have been assigned different seats in the house before the opening of this session.
In 1958, I was seated near you. In 1959, a change sent me to your extreme right and I now find myself to your left. You will admit, Mr. Speaker, that it has been quite a trip for me in so little time. But after all, those changes were not made as a result of a general election and my distinguished leader, the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) is still at the helm.
This year, I shall hardly be able to observe from here the pale and often abashed faces

The Address-Mr. Allard of the opposition members. But, on the other hand, I shall easily see face to face the ministers and the parliamentary secretaries of whom all the people of Canada speak so well.
I wish that in a coming session, my colleagues who have also crossed to this side of the house get a seat nearer to that of the Prime Minister, therefore a more profitable
seat.
I take this opportunity, Mr. Speaker, of
heartily congratulating the new ministers, the parliamentary secretaries, as well as the Deputy Speaker.
The Minister of Public Works (Mr. Walker) will understand that a good lawyer could not do without the services of a professional engineer in drawing up preliminary plans for many projects.
As to the Associate Minister of National Defence (Mr. Sevigny), he has been preparing himself for a long time for his responsibilities with regard to defence and fighting, for when he left his brilliant military career he wrote a book which, if my memory serves me right, bears the title: "Facing the Enemy". I am therefore convinced that hon. members of the opposition will suffer many a reverse if they dare to lay an ambush for him.
There should also be a word of welcome for two new members of this house. One of them, who represents the riding of Hastings-Frontenac (Mr. Webb), succeeds a very cultured minister. The other (Mr. Tardif) represents the constituency of Russell. Because he waited, Mr. Speaker, until his party went into opposition before he set out to win votes, this hon. member, to my mind, took action too tardily.
Mr. Speaker, without forgetting to congratulate the mover and seconder of the address in reply to the speech from the throne, who have fulfilled their task with much competence and brilliancy, I should like, tonight, to raise a matter referred to in the speech from the throne, one which is not only of current interest, but also of national and international concern. I refer to the problem of disarmament and its economic consequences.
Modern weapons have put mankind in a perfectly paradoxical situation. The more man conquers nature, the more he dominates matter, the greater in his heart the feeling of insecurity.
With the success that science has brought him, man seems to have forgotten the great spiritual values which give human life its justification, and which can only develop in an atmosphere of freedom and respect for the human being.
Because men feel more insecure, the question of disarmament has become their major

problem. There have been talks on disarmament for the past 13 years at the United Nations. Between 1946 and 1951, the great powers have discussed all aspects of disarmament in both organizations, the atomic energy commission and the conventional armaments commission.
Having failed to reach agreement, both organizations were dissolved in 1952, and the disarmament committee was set up. The great powers then began a round of endless negotiations, but again in 1953, a deadlock having been reached in the committee, the general assembly recommended the creation of a subcommittee. The disarmament subcommittee met in 1954, 1955, 1956 and 1957, alternatively in New York and in London.
While the disarmament committee, set up under a general assembly resolution passed on January 11, 1952, was composed of representatives of members of the security council and of the Canadian delegate, the subcommittee, set up on April 19,	1954,
included delegates from Canada, the United States, France, Great Britain and the U.S.S.R. Throughout those monotonous years, the work done by the committee was essentially a job of negotiation. Delegates analysed, explored and broke ground in every direction. The volume containing the minutes of their meetings staggers the imagination.
Either before the agencies I have just mentioned, or before the security council, or the general assembly, or the first commission of the United Nations, more than 900 meetings were held, with no success in bringing any degree of disarmament. On the contrary, during the last 12 years the countries have accumulated enormous stocks of increasingly developed and destructive weapons. To quote but one example, NATO members have spent, since 1950, more than $420 billion in armaments.
But today, following recent events, hopes have not died out and we may believe even in the possibility of total disarmament. You know, Mr. Speaker, that a new study group of ten members will resume this work in Geneva next March 15. This commission has the privilege of parity between both the opposed blocks; for it includes five communist countries and five countries of western mind. For the west, those countries are the United States, Great Britain, France, Italy and Canada; the communist bloc is represented by the U.S.S.R., Poland, Czechoslovakia, Rumania and Albania.
This commission of ten will act somehow outside the United Nations, who will send reports to this group, and get suggestions in return.

Moreover, during the fourteenth regular session of the political commission of the general assembly of the United Nations the east and the west just reached a significant agreement following a joint resolution with regard to disarmament, by accepting to refer every disarmament problem to the commission of ten.
The basic issues with regard to disarmament deal with the cessation of nuclear arms production, destruction of existing stocks and gradual reduction of armaments of every kind, all within the framework of an efficient inspection and control system.
For several years, the east and the west have recognized that experiments with regard to nuclear arms should be stopped. The point on which they were in disagreement was the duration of such suspension. On various occasions, they expressed views in common, with regard to either the necessity of slowing down the armament race, or the prohibition of nuclear arms or again the cessation of experimental explosions.
For its part, Canada has always felt that a well balanced disarmament is an objective that can only be reached step by step. Suspension of nuclear tests would be, in many ways, a valuable first step in the right direction; it could eventually stop those tests permanently, and control measures put into effect for that purpose could constitute an experiment of international scientific cooperation of the first magnitude, paving the way to control of other more complex aspects of disarmament.
It is known that small nations feel they are just spectators. They cannot content themselves with this role, because they too are, in all respects, exposed to the consequences of the armaments race. Furthermore, they are exposed to resulting dangers, without any means of eluding them, whereas the great powers responsible for creating those dangers are perhaps also able to discover means of guarding themselves against them. In this connection, we may assume that in case of nuclear war, all that would befall the great powers would be the consequences of their own acts, while small nations would suffer through no fault of their own.
The concern of the great powers is rather political and based on their own interests, while that of the small nations is humanitarian in character, being based on the interests of mankind. The threat of war being world-wide, small nations cannot be regarded as mere spectators, because their people form the majority of the world's population.
More than ever, world opinion favours an end to nuclear tests. On June 11, 1958, the
The Address-Mr. Allard News Chronicle, a British newspaper, wrote that in a world public opinion poll concerning the ending of nuclear tests, the number of people in favour of such a move was 90 per cent in Delhi, 82 per cent in Oslo, 79 per cent in Vienna, 70 per cent in Paris and Athens, 69 per cent in Helsinki, 68 per cent in Brussels and 62 per cent in London.
Experts increasingly agree that the continuation of nuclear and thermonuclear tests can cause irreparable harm to all of mankind.
Many of the most prominent scientists of the world, including some of the most reputed of the United States, agree that each test of nuclear weapons produces an amount of radioactivity that spreads in the atmosphere. This radioactivity, as a future fall-out, may drop anywhere in the world. It is also recognized that the amount of fall-out varies according to the size of the bomb, the height of the explosion above ground level and other conditions.
Practically all scientists in the world agree that this radioactivity rises into the stratosphere in the shape of strontium 90-an element which has a very long chemical life- gradually falls back to earth over a period which may last for many years, and is then assimilated by animal and plant life. Strontium 90 can not only increase the incidence of cancer, but also affect future generations.
Mr. Speaker, would the hon. member allow a question? In order to break the monotony of his reading, could he give us the page and paragraph he has now reached?
You chose a bad moment to break the monotony.

Mr. Speaker, I tried, at the beginning of my remarks, to keep to issues which might seriously interest all Canadians, and I am sorry that I must, at this stage, make a digression in order to say that, this afternoon, I had the opportunity of listening to the speech of the hon. member for Nickel Belt (Mr. Godin) whose statements certainly were consistent with those of the other hon. members of the Liberal opposition which I heard yesterday and which I read as reported in the papers. As a matter of fact, I must say that the speeches in particular of the hon. members for Nickel Belt and Hull (Mr. Caron) were a great disappointment, not only to this house but to the whole Canadian people.

The Address-Mr. Allard
Indeed, we find that members of the opposition are now very talkative. They suggest to the House of Commons and to the whole Canadian nation, bills about which they had kept silent when they were in power; which means that they have waited until they would be in the opposition to consider these issues, and that is why, in my opinion, they are to blame. The points brought up yesterday by the hon. member for Hull in particular, who told us he was happy-though astonished-that the government of the province of Quebec would consider the possibility of the repatriation of the Canadian constitution. His astonishment is easy to explain. For, within the Canadian confederation of 1960, we know- and by we I mean the people of my province-that as between the federal government and the government of the province of Quebec, there are two governments who know all the respect due to the union agreements, who understand the causes-
Hear. Hear.

Therefore I am not surprised, Mr. Speaker, to see the flexibility and the constructive way with which both the federal government and the government of the province of Quebec work together brilliantly towards the realization of certain projects and in seeking a solution to the many great and complicated problems now brought up by the Liberal opposition and which existed when the members of the opposition were in power.
If the hon. member for Nickel Belt will let me carry on, I shall continue my remarks on the problem of disarmament.
To quote statements made by prominent atomic scientists at a conference held in Central hall, Westminster, in London, during the last week of 1958, I must point out that every large scale nuclear test represents the premeditated murder of 15,000 unborn children, not to mention the harm done to their parents. Nobody can know how many other genetic disasters can be caused in this manner. Physically, morally and intellectually, a man-eating tiger cannot be transformed into a domesticated cat. It is also impossible to make the hydrogen bomb harmless. Apart from all other considerations, common sense requires that this death march be given up.
The United Nations scientific committee report on the effects of ionizing radiations confirms the widespread fear and anxiety with regard to the effects of radiations. Therefore, as I have just said, the problem is clear enough.
A total of 9,234 scientists from all over the world have made a moving appeal in favour

of the suspension of nuclear tests. Professor Pauling, prominent Nobel prize winner of the United States, has already depicted with much eloquence and detail the positive and irreparable damages of atomic explosions.
For the safety of the whole humanity, disarmament is an urgent and vital problem that must be solved by an efficient system of international control.
The system that has been looked into by the experts in Geneva in 1958 would require the establishment of an international control agency; the development, the testing and the acceptation of various equipment; the choice of the most appropriate sites for control stations and their distribution in a system covering the whole world; the establishment of a safe communications system; an agency for the analysis and use of the observations made by the control stations; the recruiting of the staff and other necessary arrangements. All this is listed in the experts' report. Experts are thinking in terms of a chain of stations separated by distances varying from 1,000 to 3,500 kilometres. There would be from 160 to 170 land stations and about ten seaborne stations. Furthermore, scientists have not failed to indicate that the exact number of control stations could only be determined during the very process of their establishment around the globe, as geographical and weather conditions would permit.
Today, an efficient control of the cessation of nuclear tests is therefore considered as physically possible. It is only then that we shall be able to judge the good faith of the Russians who, in the past, have always demanded total disarmament before international control, whose efficiency they did not trust very much.
It should be remembered that control is not an end but a means. The end is the absolute refusal to resort to atomic weapons; the means resides in control. Prohibition without control makes no sense. Where there's a will, there's a way. Whoever wants to achieve prohibition must logically and unavoidably propose and accept control.
Control has become today the executive organ and the guarantee of the observation of the majority of multilateral conventions. Also, control is legal from the point of view of international law. To refuse it or to postpone its application would be to deny the remarkable progress achieved by international law and legal science in the last few years.
Does not control appear as definite evidence of the sincerity of purpose and good faith of the parties concerned? It may create or

re-establish confidence. While control brings to mind a legal fact, confidence is actually a mood.
Besides, this control is not contrary to the principle of the sovereignty of the state, for I believe sovereignty is the authority of the state in the midst of the international community. In view of a modern fact, that is the existence of a community of nations, it is impossible to assert that the state is absolutely supreme, that its sovereignty is independent from the evolution of the international community.
As long as no system of control will be established by an agreement, negotiations should go on, preferably under the sponsorship of the United Nations, in order to achieve the gradual suspension of the production and manufacture, as well as the destruction and gradual transformation of the accumulated stocks, on an equal and reciprocal basis.
In studying the disarmament problem, you have to consider the economic implications.
It is just as important to consider the means of ensuring the discharge of 20 million people from the armed forces, of the various countries, and their integration into the national economy, as well as the transfer of the tremendous amounts invested in armament production into such new fields as consumer goods.
Certainly, you cannot change from a wartime to a peacetime economy overnight at the national level. There must first be an agreement at the international level covering the economic field. It is only after an agreement has been reached on such problems that a wartime economy can shift to peacetime economy on a national level.
Such is disarmament as we see it, with all its difficulties and its new problems. It calls for a constant display of realism. If we really want to help not only this generation, but future generations as well, we must have greater patience, greater strength of purpose, and unfailing courage, because patience and strength of purpose are the basis of negotiations. Even when a good start has been made, serious and practical negotiations involving the contribution of scientific experts will still be required to achieve the objectives of the peoples of the world.
We believe that any practical progress towards the solution of disarmament problems can be achieved only by stages, with a clear recognition of the need for over-all balanced planning at each stage, in view of the close connection between the various aspects of
The Address-Mr. Boivin disarmament. The powers mainly responsible for maintaining peace and security should recognize and practise honestly and sincerely the basic truth that, in the present state of the world, true disarmament measures should be accompanied by a system of effective safeguards, that is to say, a system of international inspection and control.
There was a time when the peoples of the earth had a choice between peace and war. Today, because of the destructive power of nuclear weapons, the world must choose between peace or annihilation. Let us pray the Lord that the men of good will succeed in making reason triumph over bestiality.
The day that disarmament becomes a reality, we will have to have more respect for the rights and basic freedoms of the individual, because the deep cause of war has always been the violation of those rights and freedoms. That is why we are quite in favour of the adoption of a Canadian bill of rights during this federal session, while in 1960, international agencies will earnestly try to bring about total disarmament.
Our beautiful Canada, one of the ten members of the new commission on disarmament, is called upon to play a part of prime importance, and as the Secretary of State for External Affairs, (Mr. Green) said on October 31, 1959:
Our country is now considered as an international power and its particular role is to help the smaller nations and to advise the greater powers.

Mr. Speaker, once more the Canadian people have witnessed on television on Thursday January 14, 1960, the opening of the third session of the twenty fourth parliament.
I would again, Mr. Speaker, pay you a tribute on behalf of the people in the riding I have the honour to represent. I want to add that we, in the opposition, admire the tactful and able way in which you direct our debates in this house.
I note that, after your last trip abroad, you seem rested, which we are happy to see. I am therefore taking the opportunity to congratulate you on the way you represent this country. Your trip which has taken you to Lebanon, together with your charming wife, increased the prestige of Canada among that people, and I am all the prouder of it because it happened that one of my fellow citizens of Granby was a witness to your visit and had the great honour to meet you on that occasion.

The Address-Mr. Boivin
I reminded hon. members in this house last year that my home town was celebrating its centenary. As a matter of fact, during the twelve months which just came to an end, we have tried, by means of religious and civic festivities, to pay a tribute to the founders of the city of Granby as well as to all who contributed from near or far to the success of that anniversary. Therefore, as I am their representative in this house, I would like to express my thanks and my gratitude to them.
Granby was honoured to receive many visitors who came from all parts of this country.
The Prime Minister was so kind as to accept our invitation to visit the gem of the eastern townships, right after the second session, that is last July. By his presence, he wanted to show his appreciation to the people of that town which, like all the others, contributed to the development of Canada, and on behalf of all the people of Granby I want to express to him our gratitude, Mr. Speaker.
The centenary celebrations ended on a grand note at the end of November with the visit of the Queen's representative, accompanied by the hostess of Rideau Hall. We were extremely proud to welcome them, and it is easy to see why the men and women of my constituency felt all the more honoured at this visit considering the many duties to be discharged by the Governor General upon his appointment to this high office by her gracious majesty. In return for the honour he paid us, we pray the Lord to give him a long life.
I was present in the Senate, Mr. Speaker, to hear the speech from the throne, which was short and which His Excellency read with the greatest diginity.
I extend congratulations in customary fashion to the mover of the address in reply to the speech from the throne for the honor bestowed upon him, an honour which is reflected on the constituency of Rimouski which he represents. He did try, in his way, to show that Canada is prosperous, but he will not be surprised if I say that many of my constituents do not share his opinion.
We all witnessed a historical event in listening to the seconder of the address.
The hon. member for Grenville-Dundas (Mrs. Casselman) paid a tribute to her constituency, and under the circumstances, she deserves our full admiration. May I add that the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. 
Rowe), a former member of the Conservative cabinet, was doubly honoured, this time as a private member, in hearing the maiden speech of the hon. member. I venture to say it is the first time since confederation that a father had the honour to hear his daughter seconding the address.
I also wish to congratulate the hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Flynn) for his appointment as chairman of committees. Having had the honour of meeting him personally since he came to the house, I am convinced that he will be worthy of the functions entrusted to him.
I should like to associate myself with my colleagues in welcoming the new member for Hastings-Frontenac (Mr. Webb) and in extending the most cordial welcome to the new member for Russell (Mr. Tardif).
The Canadian government paid tribute, once again, to the constituency of Longueuil in making its representative Associate Minister of National Defence. I extend to him my congratulations and best wishes for success. May I add that his sincere support of the Prime Minister has finally got him a double reward.
Mr. Speaker, I congratulate the new Minister of Public Works (Mr. Walker) and I add that we hope to find in him the same cordiality we found in his predecessors.
My most sincere congratulations to the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) for the straight-forward and sincere outline he gave the house in reply to the speech from the throne, showing once again that he wants to carry out for the time being and with tenacity the task entrusted to him. I should like to add that, for purely political motives, our leader was unfairly criticized by the government side, and I must say personally that there is no member of our party who is not immensely proud of him. Besides, if I glance on the other side of the house, I cannot see anyone who would be worthy of deserving the Nobel prize or be one of the "three wise men" of international politics. His role in history has been guaranteed and approved in advance by all well-thinking statesmen of the world. Moreover, I should like to quote the words of one of my Anglo-Saxon friends: "There is nothing small about him". Would to heaven that some day I could say as much of those who are sitting across the floor!
Our leader extended words of welcome to the Minister of Finance, and I should like to do the same.
You will admit, Mr. Speaker, that it was surprising to hear the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) make the following remark

in this house about the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson), as reported on page 52 of Hansard:

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I will say again that the hon. gentleman does not know what he is talking about.
I was all the more surprised considering the great respect he has for the author of this remark.
Mr. Speaker, I should like to refer to the remarks made in this house by the Minister of Finance on February 22, 1950, in the debate on the speech from the throne. I quote from page 137 of Hansard:
Mr. Speaker, the house has listened to a very important and interesting statement from the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson). Since we in this part of the house have sought at all times to keep our external affairs on a non-partisan basis, perhaps the house will fully understand me when I say that if in this country we must, unfortunately, it seems, for the next several years, have a Liberal administration, nevertheless we are very glad that in that Liberal administration the portfolio of external affairs is in the very capable hands of Mike Pearson.
I fully realize that in 1950, the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) never expected to hold his present office, nor did he expect to become the right-hand man of the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker). Had he expected that, I am sure he would have had a different line of reasoning. Deep inside, I know that if he did not have to follow the policies of the Conservative party, he would pay him the same tribute as Leader of the Opposition.
Having read the remarks made by the Minister of Finance on August 21, 1950, it must be admitted that in the Conservative party, when you change places, you change faces.
I note, Mr. Speaker, that the Minister of Justice (Mr. Fulton) is not in his seat. I should like to quote some words spoken in this house by the minister in 1948, because the same words might well be used today as comment on the brief speech from the throne. I quote this from page 1845 of Hansard for March 3, 1948, second last paragraph:
It Is now nearly three months since the address in reply to the speech from the throne was first moved in this house, and the aspect which I wish to discuss this afternoon for a few minutes is not the address itself but the amendment to it that we are debating, because that amendment is, in effect, a vote of want of confidence in the government. It is, therefore, important to go over the speech from the throne, which we are now considering, and find out why it is that we of the official opposition consider that the program there set forth, coupled with the government's past record, is not such as to command the confidence of the house.

Mr. Speaker, I regard as a privilege the opportunity to participate in this debate. The throne speech debate is often referred to by the press as a dull, drab affair. I find it quite the contrary; indeed, I think it very interesting and informative to hear members from all parts of the country presenting their views on a great range of subjects. I think

it underlines very well the representative aspect of our responsible, representative, democratic form of parliamentary government.
I find myself in a new location in this house. The hon. member who just concluded his remarks spoke about changing places and changing faces. It is quite a feat to move from one side of the house to the other, but I have accomplished a move from one end to the other. It is quite a drastic move, but I assure the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) that I am under no illusion about this, for I do not intend to mistake movement for progress. I will, however, refuse to regard it as regression.
I should like to join my colleagues, sir in extending good wishes to you upon your election to your office. I should like to express my good wishes to your deputy the hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Rea) for whom we entertain such a high regard.
I listened with great appreciation to the hon. member for Rimouski (Mr. Morissette) and the hon. member for Grenville-Dundas (Mrs. Casselman) during their splendid contributions to the debate as they moved and seconded the address. I was impressed by the seconder's references to our historical development and by her interest in the centennial celebrations of 1967. We Canadians are not notably an historically minded people. Perhaps this is the reason that, at times, our nationalism seems to be somewhat sporadic and perhaps a bit tenuous. Although still a young country we have now had nearly a century of our confederation, and we have had a much longer record of political and social organization to our credit. I think it behooves us, as a people, to know and to honour our past. The great Joseph Howe said:
A wise nation preserve's its records, gathers up its monuments, decorates the tombs of its illustrious dead, repairs its great public structures, and fosters national pride and love of country by perpetual reference to the sacrifices and glories of the past.
With that thought in mind I should like to congratulate the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Walker). I think the decision made to name the new building for the fisheries and public work departments after Sir Charles Tupper is a most happy one. That great father of confederation should certainly be remembered. With the hon. member for Grenville-Dundas (Mrs. Casselman) I am happy that the Prime Minister is one of those deeply interested in the history of our land and its institution. I think we can be assured that he and his government will plan imaginatively for the centennial celebration. I am particularly deeply concerned about

this matter, Mr. Speaker, because I have the honour to represent that constituency where confederation began.
In Prince Edward Island, in the capital city of Charlottetown in 1864, a group of colonial delegates held the first meeting in that series which culminated in the agreement upon the Quebec resolutions upon which our federal structure has subsequently been based. Just as the 1864 meeting was a preview and a forerunner of Canadian confederation, so I think will the 1964 celebration of that event be a forerunner and a most valuable prelude and preview to the larger and greater celebration which will take place in 1967 all across the land. I very much hope that the dominion government and the members of the House of Commons will interest themselves in the plans which are afoot already for the Charlottetown celebration. Perhaps some tangible evidence of the dominion government's interest in this matter might well be forthcoming. I would not think of filling out the details, but such a thing as a museum of eastern colonial history or a cultural centre or something equally significant might mark in a very special way this important event in our national story.
On this subject I should like to applaud the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources (Mr. Hamilton) because his department has recognized the old site of Fort Amherst in the harbour of Charlottetown and the old French settlement of Fort La Joie. We now have there a national historic park. The people of my province are deeply appreciative of that park. We have quite a background of French occupation in the province of Prince Edward Island. We look upon Jacques Cartier as our first tourist. He came here in 1534 and he liked it very well. For a moment I thought I might hazard rendering in French the remarks he wrote in his logbook, but since I am not very proficient in contemporary French and am far worse in archaic French, I will translate roughly and say that he found it altogether beautiful and about as pleasant a place as it would be possible to see. We like that impression that he had and we think it is a sound one.
It is interesting-and I assure hon. members that I am not forgetting that I am not in a university classroom embarking upon a historical lecture-that quite often the main strands of political issues and economic arguments can be traced back to certain basic historical facts. When the province of Prince Edward Island in 1873, after some years of delay and after some overtures, shall we say, from Canada decided to enter confederation the representatives of that colony, the present province, had one very
The Address-Mr. Macquarrie urgent question which they put to the forefront of the agenda. Recognizing the importance of communications they insisted that the matter be looked after and that a definite promise be made by the dominion authorities. Although the province at the time was suffering from fairly serious economic disabilities and from the results of unfortunate political decisions the islanders continued to urge that the communications aspect be considered and be kept in the foreground.
They asked for and they obtained the recognition that the dominion was responsible for providing efficient and continuous communication for the province of Prince Edward Island with the mainland of Canada. Down through the years since 1873, regardless of the political complexion of the government either in the province or in the dominion, this has been the bedrock, one of the great essentials of dominion-provincial relations as far as the province of Prince Edward Island is concerned. I cannot but think how wise were the earlier political leaders in stressing this particular matter and in making it a binding term of confederation for this acute problem of communication has recurred and many times since.
It is a fascinating story, the story of communication across the strait of Northumberland. The early means was by iceboats. There were two types of passengers, namely first-class passengers and second-class passengers. The second-class passenger paid a certain amount but he was required to pull. The first-class passenger paid a good deal more to travel, not in comfort, certainly because it was anything but comfortable to cross the strait, but he was not obliged to get out to provide the motive power. Then there were the early steamboats with great uncertainty as to schedule. About 50 years ago the members of the parliament and senators from Prince Edward Island were very late in getting to Ottawa because the boats were not making their trips. When they arrived here one of them proposed the adjournment of the debate to discuss a matter of urgent public importance, and that matter was one which concerned them so greatly and bothered them so much in a personal way.
In 1911 Sir Robert Borden in his campaign came to the city of Charlottetown and he said, "If you will elect me as Prime Minister of Canada you will get a car ferry". They did and he did and the car ferry was put there. May I say that the fine old car ferry built for less than $1 million is still in operation and is still making its trips across the strait. It is a wonderful ship. Over the years there

The Address-Mr. Macquarrie have been other boats which were far more expensive. If one is interested in the value of a dollar-and we have been discussing that matter here-the present newest boat, the Abegweit, cost about $7 million. The one which was put in service in 1916 cost less than $900,000.
The latest chapter, Mr. Speaker, shall I say, on the boat situation is that a contract has been let for yet another ferry. We greatly appreciate the attitude of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Hees) who recognized our need for a new ferry and who moved quickly in that direction. The people in our province look forward to this boat, when it comes into operation in 1961.
But is all this enough? The demands for service have been increasing tremendously. At no time would I think of burdening you, Mr. Speaker, or my colleagues with a mass of statistics and certainly not at this late hour of our sitting. But one aspect of this matter might be illustrative of the magnitude of the problem which faces us. In 1933, 262,000 tons of freight were carried across this strait. In 1958 that figure had risen to 766,000 tons. In 1943-and that is as far back as I can get separate figures for automobiles-9,500 passenger automobiles were carried over and in 1958 the figure had risen to over 120,000. In 1959 we believe there has been a 10 per cent increase over the 1958 figures. It is therefore a problem to meet this growing demand, and it will grow. That is the present problem in Prince Edward Island.
We have perhaps one industry which is expandable and which is expanding, namely tourism. Our new provincial government is planning a vigorous move in this direction and we applaud them for that planning. For although our province is very small there are areas yet untouched and undeveloped. Of course the whole province is unspoiled.
We can project a vast increase, and therefore it is essential that this be provided. The communication link is a dominion responsibility clearly and solely. We are happy with the decision to build a new boat, and we know it will be very busy when it starts operating. But we must urge in the interests of the province, as well as broader interests, that still further steps be taken to meet this confederation commitment. All of the island's members of parliament have urged the building of a causeway, and we appreciate very much the support which has been given to us in this chamber.
I was much pleased at the reference of my colleague from Westmorland (Mr. Creaghan), my neighbour across the strait, when he gave support to the causeway project and even did me the honour of flattering me by quoting

me in this regard. That has not happened since the hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Chev-rier) did me a similar honour in the twenty-third parliament. I urge upon the government the construction of this final stage in the long story of island-mainland communications. I urge it because it will give us that promised efficient and continuous communication which modern conditions require. I urge it too because it is soundly economical.
I will again demur from producing statistics, but the present service is an expensive one. It is recognized that the dominion government has put forward great expenditures over the years in order to maintain this service. The capital equipment at the present time totals something like $22 million, representing the cost of boats and docks alone.
What about the operating costs? In 1958 there was a deficit of nearly $2 million, and therefore I repeat that economically the move toward building a causeway is a good and sound one. Since 1933 there has been a net loss of $25 million on this operation. I know the difficulties. I know they are tremendous, and I know that this engineering project is one of the greatest in the history of technology and engineering. We want the survey done ' thoroughly; we do not want anything which is ill-conceived or hasty, and we are happy that the minister has undertaken to make a thorough and comprehensive survey. We are pleased that the department has brought in the best experts, not only from within this country but from other countries, thoroughly competent to study every aspect of this important project.
At the same time I must point out that there is an element of urgency. Because of increasing demand the present facilities are becoming more and more inadequate. So something must be done, and I would urge that the causeway survey be pushed to its conclusion, and if it should be proven not feasible-and we hope this will not be the case-then immediate steps will have to be taken to augment and improve the existing ferry service.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, I would like to say that I am not appealing here for any provincial or regional consideration, although I would have a right to do so. I look at this as another part of a program of national development. This is something far bigger than a local enterprise. One of the things which has made me most happy in my support of the present Prime Minister (Mr. Die-fenbaker) and his government is that they have given us in the Atlantic provinces new ground for hope and new reasons for tackling our own problems with greater vigour. We

all recall the quick action which was taken with the Atlantic provinces adjustment grant and many other instances.
The hon. member for Burin-Burgeo (Mr. Carter) spoke the other day about the disappointment felt in his province some ten years after confederation. I might say that his province was not the only province in which there were feelings of disappointment from time to time. We have been disappointed quite a few times. We have seen in the development of Canada the economic fulcrum being moved further away from us, where it all began. "Westward the course of Empire ever stayed" is the old expression, and a fine one but, it sometimes does not go quite so well with some of us in the east.
It should be in the interests of national development, and it seems to me it is the duty of the national government to take the steps which are necessary to redress regional inequality and to move in the direction of establishing a greater over-all level of economic prosperity. This direction is being given by the government which I have the honour to support and which has cheered us so greatly in the Atlantic provinces. It has inspired us with confidence that, in this matter of tremendous importance to my province and others, we will have that same attitude, that same revelation of a truly national vision which will recognize the over-all importance of this development. This is not a matter upon which one seeks to make political capital.
Far be it for me to make comments about the provincial election in Prince Edward Island, but much of what took place did reflect a certain appreciation of this government's policy with respect to the Atlantic provinces. I can ask no more than the continuation of this same valued attitude, this same vigorous action and this same understanding and appreciation of our needs, our aspirations and our difficulties.
Mr. Speaker, much more might be said, but I have often shown publicly a certain fidelity to brevity and I will not depart from my adherence to it at this time.

Mr. Speaker, may I at the outset join with those who have paid their congratulations to the mover and seconder to the address in reply to the speech from the throne. They spoke with clarity and they spoke well, and it is a pleasure to join in the compliments which have been paid to them. May I also associate myself with those kind remarks of congratulation which have been offered to you, sir, and to other hon. members of this house who have been paid special honour since we last met.
The Address-Mr. Hellyer
In addition, Mr. Speaker, I wish to say how sorry I am to hear that General Charles Foulkes is retiring as chairman of the chiefs of staff. He is an officer of outstanding record, and his counsel and guidance have assisted and been invaluable to several ministers of national defence throughout these many years. The loss will be felt at national defence headquarters, and I wish to take this opportunity to express to him the gratitude of the Canadian people for his faithful, devoted and loyal service.
Of the time he allotted to the subject of defence, the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefen-baker) spent the greater part reading newspaper clippings of statements made by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson). It was very disappointing performance, and it did no credit either to his position or to the seriousness of the subject. He did spend some minutes dealing briefly with a few of the decisions taken by the government and I should like to take this opportunity to comment on those and other related matters.
The Prime Minister quoted Mr. Khrushchev's recent speech to the effect that the U.S.S.R. had a bountiful supply of rockets and missiles and that it is abandoning the manned bomber. He said this pronouncement by Mr. Khrushchev vindicated the position taken by the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Pearkes) in cancelling the F-105 Avro Arrow. The position of the Minister of Defence with regard to the subject has been neither clear nor consistent, and if hon. members will consult the record, both in Hansard and as it appears in newspaper clippings of speeches which the minister has made on the subject from coast to coast, they will find he said regularly that manned bombers continue to be the main threat against Canada and that it would continue to be so for some years to come.
The Prime Minister said the decision taken a year ago to cancel the Avro Arrow had been based on the best military advice available. Not more than two or three weeks ago, the secretary of defence of the United States, Mr. Gates, told the House of Representatives appropriation subcommittee on defence that a mix of weapons was still required. He said, furthermore, that whereas the United States is to proceed with United States Bomarc B anti-aircraft missile, it may be necessary to reappraise the situation, and that reappraisal might show the necessity of continuing to use manned interceptors in quantity because of their greater flexibility. The Minister of National Defence must set some store by what Mr. Gates said because he quoted his testimony at page 132 of

The Address-Mr. Hellyer Hansard in support of the government's decision to continue with the installation of the Bomarc B.
Another expert witness who differs from the Prime Minister is General Kuter, who is commander in chief of the North American air defence command. General Kuter, when asked about Canadian air defence squadrons, told newspapermen in Ottawa last November that he hoped the Canadian government would soon re-equip the squadrons presently using the obsolescent CF-100. He gave the same opinion in Washington the following day. It is obvious that the United States has always wanted, and counted on, Canada to replace the CF-100 with supersonic manned interceptors. As far as can be determined there never was any United States suggestion to the contrary. General Kuter's statement of last November merely brought the matter again to the urgent attention of the government and the Canadian people.
Is the advice the Prime Minister referred to better than the advice of Secretary Gates and General Kuter? If so, it is only fair that the Prime Minister should tell us the source to assist us in reaching our own conclusions.
You know better than that.

It is not necessarily true that United States military advisers are better than ours, even though we rely on them heavily for military intelligence reports. If there is a difference of opinion, however, it is worth while to compare both opinions carefully in order to make sure that so far as possible the one chosen is the best.

The government may have come to the conclusion that it is futile to arm against the manned bomber. If it has reached that decision, we should be told. If it has reached that decision, it should never have decided to go ahead with the Bomarc installations in the first place or, at least, it should cancel the plan forthwith.
The Bomarc is a weapon designed to be used against the manned bomber. It has no function against ballistic missiles. Its role, though not identical with that of the interceptor has the same functions as the manned interceptor against the possibility of attack by manned bombers. If, however, the government has not reached that decision but still holds the view that it is necessary to maintain a defence against the manned bomber until the Russian inventory is depleted, then it should long ago have made a concrete plan to re-equip the air defence squadrons with new supersonic interceptors. The government cannot have it both ways. The Bomarc, by itself, is useless; it is only one of a family of weapons. It only makes sense as a second line to the manned interceptor.
I tried to make this point during the estimates last summer but it is difficult to make much impression on this government. The Minister of National Defence said he subscribed to the theory of defence in depth, but he does not back this belief by action. He should tell us now whether the government still subscribes to the theory of defence in depth with respect to the North American continent or whether it does not.
May I call it ten o'clock?

ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS	EGG PRODUCER STATISTICS
The following answers, deposited with the Clerk of the house, are printed in the official report of debates pursuant to standing order 39:

1.	Was any loss sustained by the government from the sale of 10,000,000 pounds of butter for export to Britain in October, 1959? If so, in what amount?
2.	What was the basis of arriving at the price of 56 cents per pound for the sale of this butter?
3.	What are the names of the Canadian exporters to whom the government sold this butter?
Answer by: Hon. D. S. Harkness (Minister of
Agriculture):
1.	Yes. Butter sold for export was acquired by the stabilization board at a cost based on 64 cents delivered Montreal. Butter acquired by the board is resold in the domestic market at the purchase price, i.e., 64 cents basis Montreal, with the board absorbing carrying charges. The difference between the resale value in the domestic market and the export price was approximately 8 cents a pound.
2.	Butter was sold by tender.
3.	Black Diamond Cheese Ltd., Canada Packers Limited., George Hodge & Son., Lovell & Christmas.

Answer by: Hon. D. S. Harkness (Minister of
Agriculture):

Question No. 42-Mr. Boulanger:
1.	How many producers of eggs are there in Canada?
2.	How many producers of eggs have registered at the grading establishments in Canada?
Answer by: Hon. D. S. Harkness (Minister of Agriculture):
1.	The 1956 census gives a total of 347,553 farms with laying hens.
2.	78,296 egg producers were registered at January 15, 1960.
